       Dear Secretary Bose:

              Southern Company Services, Inc. (“SCS”), acting on its own behalf and as agent for Alabama
       Power Company, Georgia Power Company, Mississippi Power Company, and Southern Power
       Company, hereby submits, for informational purposes only,1 the annual informational filing required
       under the Southern Company System Intercompany Interchange Contract (“IIC”).2

              On May 9, 2022, SCS filed the current version of the IIC (“Amended and Restated IIC”) in
       Docket No. ER22-1820-000.3 The Amended and Restated IIC was accepted for filing by the
       Commission in a letter order dated July 11, 2022, with the effective date of July 13, 2022 supplied in a
       subsequent filing.4 SCS is submitting a complete copy of the informational filing in PDF format and is

===== DKT 56765 STF-JKA-10-11&12 PD/STF-JKA-10-12 Attachment B PUBLIC DISCLOSURE.docx =====

STF-JKA-10-12 Attachment B — Marginal Cost of Transmission Methodology
This document provides a description of the methodology for calculating the marginal cost of transmission and also serves as a companion to the calculation spreadsheets for 2023 through 2025 helping to connect each step to the corresponding tab and column. The marginal cost of transmission for 2023 through 2025 includes the Average Incremental Cost (“AIC”) methodology. Starting in 2025, a 500kV marginal cost adder is included with the AIC to represent the marginal cost of transmission. Please note, the AIC workbook itself was laid out differently in each year, so the tab and column names change from year to year.
Steps for Calculating the Average Incremental Cost (AIC):
Load is increased at a substation until the first transmission constraint is identified.
A transmission project is then estimated and implemented in the case to alleviate that first constraint.
Load is then further increased at that substation until a second transmission constraint is identified.
The estimated cost of the transmission project is divided by the load growth enabled by the transmission project between the first and second constraints.
The spreadsheets that have been provided for each of the requested years complete each of the four steps described above, one row at a time, for hundreds of locations, and then averages the results to represent the marginal cost of transmission for the respective year.
Example of AIC Calculation:
Substation Alpha currently feeds a load of 50 MW. The loading at the substation is increased until a nearby transmission line overloads due to the growth; this occurs at 71 MW. The overloaded transmission line operates at 230kV and is 1.6 miles long. The average cost to reconductor a 230kV line is $1.25M/mile. Reconductoring the constraint would cost $2M.


Load continues to grow at Substation Alpha until it reaches 86 MW, at which point, a second nearby transmission line overloads. The $2M project created 15 MW of additional capacity at Substation Alpha.


Repeat the steps above and average across each substation with load represented in the planning model across the Southern Company footprint to arrive at the AIC $/kW.  

Steps for Calculating the 500kV Marginal Cost Adder:
Due to the recent significant load growth, there is now a need to expand the 500kV transmission system. To account for the 500kV system, a 500kV marginal cost adder was developed and introduced in 2025. The 500kV Marginal Cost Adder is calculated by summing the costs of all 500kV projects in the Ten-Year Plan and dividing it by the load growth utilizing Year 10 of the current vintage of cases and Year 1 of the previous vintage of cases.
500kW Marginal Cost Adder Calculation:


Marginal Cost of Transmission Calculation:


2023 Calculation (AIC only)
Where Each Step Happens in the AIC Spreadsheet
File: STF-JKA-10-12 Attachment C
The 2023 AIC workbook is laid out across several tabs. The “FCITCs” tab lists the constraints each location hits, in order (Constraint #1, #2, #3 ...). The “Calculations” tab prices the fix for each constraint and works out the dollars-per-kW between successive constraints. The “Estimates” tab holds the unit-cost price list, and “Branch_Data” is the raw equipment data from the power-system model. Reading across the “FCITCs” and “Calculations” tabs for one location shows all four steps in order.
Step
Where to look (tab / column)
What it means in plain terms
Step 1 - Increase load until the first constraint appears
Tab: FCITCsThe “Constraint #1” block - column “#1 FCITC”
“#1 FCITC” is the amount of extra load (in megawatts) the location can absorb before the very first piece of equipment reaches its limit (i.e., the first constraint). The “Load Bus Sink” column names the substation; “#1 From kV / #1 To kV / #1 Type” name the line or transformer that hit its limit first, and “#1 Contingency” is the outage that caused it.
Step 2 - Estimate and add a project to fix that first constraint
Tab: Calculations (unit prices on the “Estimates” tab)Columns “#1 Miles” and “#1 Cost ($ M)”
“#1 Cost ($ M)” is the estimated cost of the project that relieves the first constraint. It uses the standard per-mile and per-unit prices listed on the “Estimates” tab (the 2022 PEP price list - for example, about REDACTED of 115kV line or REDACTED of 500kV line), multiplied by the size of the fix (“#1 Miles”).
Step 3 - Keep increasing load until a second constraint appears
Tab: FCITCsThe “Constraint #2” block - column “#2 FCITC”
With the first fix assumed to be in place, load keeps growing until the next piece of equipment reaches its limit. That second constraint (the “second constraint”) is captured in the “Constraint #2” block, with “#2 FCITC” holding the higher load level.
Step 4 - Divide project cost by the load growth it unlocked
Tab: CalculationsColumns “#1 -> #2 Load Growth (MW)” and “#1 -> #2 ($/kW)”
The load unlocked between the first and second constraints is the “#1 -> #2 Load Growth (MW)” column, and the “#1 -> #2 ($/kW)” column divides the project cost by that load growth to give the dollars-per-kilowatt result for that location. (The sheet also carries the same math out to later constraints - #2 -> #3, #3 -> #4, and so on but the first-to-second result is the one PRICEM uses.)

Bringing the results together: After every location has its dollars-per-kW result, the “Calculations .1 Cutoff” tab narrows to the values used, and the “PRICEM Input .1 Cutoff” tab combines them: it removes statistical outliers and averages what remains (an “Avg. w/o Outliers” of about REDACTED). After adjusting for inflation, the resulting value is REDACTED for 2023.


2024 Calculation (AIC only)
Where Each Step Happens in the AIC Spreadsheet
File: STF-JKA-10-12 Attachment D
The 2024 AIC workbook has three tabs. The “Calculations” tab does all the step-by-step work. Each row is one location on the system, and reading a row left to right shows all four steps in order. The “Summary” tab combines the results, and “Inc. Load Graph” plots them.
Step
Where to look (tab / column)
What it means in plain terms
Step 1 - Increase load until the first constraint appears
Tab: CalculationsColumn “FCITC #1”
FCITC #1 is the amount of extra load (in megawatts) the location can absorb before the very first piece of equipment reaches its limit (the “first constraint”). The “Bus” column names the substation where the load was added, and the “From kV / To kV / Type” columns name the specific line or transformer that hit its limit first.
Step 2 - Estimate and add a project to fix that first constraint
Tab: CalculationsColumns “Type,” “Cost_Lookup,” “Cost,” “LINLEN,” and “Project Cost”
Once the limiting piece of equipment is known, the sheet estimates what it costs to fix it. “Cost” is a standard unit price for that kind of equipment (for example, a mile of 115kV line or a 230kV transformer), identified by the matching label in the “Cost_Lookup” column. “LINLEN” is the line length in miles, and “Project Cost” multiplies the unit price by the size of the fix to get the estimated cost (in millions of dollars).
Step 3 - Keep increasing load until a second constraint appears
Tab: CalculationsColumn “FCITC #2”
With the fix from Step 2 assumed to be in place, load keeps growing until the next piece of equipment reaches its limit. FCITC #2 is that higher load level - the second transmission constraint.
Step 4 - Divide project cost by the load growth it unlocked
Tab: CalculationsColumns “TDF,” “Incremental Load,” and “dollar_per_kW”
The extra load the project unlocked is the difference between the second and first constraints (FCITC #2 minus FCITC #1), shown in the “Incremental Load” column. “TDF” describes how much of the added load actually flows over the limiting equipment, and the final “dollar_per_kW” column divides the Project Cost by the Incremental Load to give the answer for that location: dollars per kilowatt of new load.

Bringing the results together: After every location has its own dollars-per-kW result, the “Summary” tab combines them: it removes statistical outliers, averages what remains (an “Average excluding Outliers” of about REDACTED for 2024), and after adjusting for inflation, the resulting value is REDACTED for 2024. The “Inc. Load Graph” tab simply plots these results.  

2025 Calculation (AIC + 500kV adder)
Where Each Step Happens in the AIC Spreadsheet
File: STF-JKA-10-12 Attachment E
The AIC workbook's two working tabs are “Full Calculations Input” and “PRICEM Input no Outliers”. Both have the same columns; the second one simply drops a few extreme outlier results before averaging. Each row is one location on the system. Read a single row left to right and you see all four steps happen in order.
Step
Where to look (tab / column)
What it means in plain terms
Step 1 - Increase load until the first constraint appears
Tab: Full Calculations Input / PRICEM Input no OutliersColumn “FCITC #1”
FCITC #1 is the amount of extra load (in megawatts) the location can absorb before the very first piece of equipment reaches its limit (i.e., the first constraint), the point where the first transmission constraint shows up. The “Load Bus Sink” column names the substation where the load was added, and the “From kV / To kV / Type” columns name the specific line or transformer that hit its limit first.
Step 2 - Estimate and add a project to fix that first constraint
Tab: Full Calculations Input / PRICEM Input no OutliersColumns “Type,” “Cost_Lookup,” “Cost,” “LINLEN,” and “Project Cost”
Once the limiting piece of equipment is known, the sheet estimates what it costs to fix it. “Cost” is a standard unit price for that kind of equipment (for example, a mile of 115kV line or a 230kV transformer), carried in the “Cost” column and identified by the matching label in the “Cost_Lookup” column. “LINLEN” is the line length in miles. “Project Cost” multiplies the unit price by the size of the fix to get the estimated cost (in millions of dollars) of the upgrade that relieves the first constraint.

The extra load the project unlocked is the difference between the second and first constraints (FCITC #2 minus FCITC #1), and it is shown in the “Incremental Load” column. The final column, “dollar_per_kW,” divides the Project Cost by the Incremental Load to give the answer for that location: dollars per kilowatt of new load.

Bringing the results together: After every location has its own dollars-per-kW result, the “Statistical Summary” tab combines them. The “Inc Load Graph” tab plots these results, and the “Branch Data” tab is the raw equipment data exported from the power-system model.

Where Each Step Happens in the 500kV Spreadsheet
File: STF-JKA-10-12 Attachment F
The 500kV spreadsheet answers the same question: How much does it cost to serve one more kilowatt of load - but for the high-voltage 500kV “backbone” of the system rather than for one local substation. Because 500kV projects are large and regional, they are not tied to a single substation with one line hitting a limit. Instead, the same four steps are applied to the whole 500kV system at once: the region’s set of needed 500kV projects stands in for the “project,” and the region’s expected load growth stands in for the load unlocked between constraints. The steps line up like this:
Step
Where to look (tab / column)
What it means in plain terms
Step 1 - Load grows until the system needs reinforcement
Tab: 2024 TYP 500 KV Projects (with GA Projects / AL Projects detail)The project list (“Project Name,” “Project Sponsor,” “Need Date”)
Each row on the “2024 TYP 500 KV Projects” tab is a real, planned 500kV project that was identified because growing load and system needs pushed the “backbone” to a limit. In other words, the whole list represents the points where the 500kV system reached its “first constraint” and needed to be reinforced.
Step 2 - Estimate and include the projects that fix those needs
Tab: 2024 TYP 500 KV Projects, summarized on 500kV Marginal Cost AdderColumns “Total Cost,” “Include (Y=1, N=0),” and “Adjusted Cost”
“Total Cost” is the estimated cost of each 500kV project. The “Include (Y=1, N=0)” column controls which projects count, and a contingency adjustment produces the “Adjusted Cost.” The included, adjusted costs are added up and carried onto the “500kV Marginal Cost Adder” tab as the “2024 TYP 500kV Cost” line - about REDACTED of total 500kV investment.
Step 3 - Measure how much load that investment supports
Tab: Load, summarized on 500kV Marginal Cost AdderThe “Load” and “Load Growth” lines
The “Load” tab tracks the region's forecasted peak load year by year. On the “500kV Marginal Cost Adder” tab, the “Load” line shows the starting and ending forecast (about REDACTED growing to about  REDACTED ), and the “Load Growth” line is the difference – about REDACTED (REDACTED). That load growth is the 500kV equivalent of the gap between the first and second constraints.
Step 4 - Divide total project cost by the load growth it supports
Tab: 500kV Marginal Cost AdderThe “500 kV Marginal Adder” and “Total Marginal Cost” lines
Just like the AIC sheet divides one project’s cost by the load it unlocks, this tab divides the total 500kV investment (about REDACTED ) by the total load growth (about REDACTED). The result is the “500 kV Marginal Adder,” about REDACTED. The same tab then adds the AIC value (about REDACTED, on the “Average Incremental Marginal Cost” line) to that adder to give the “Total Marginal Cost” line, about REDACTED, the value provided for 2025.

How the 500kV method differs from the AIC method: The AIC sheet performs the four steps literally, one substation and one row at a time. The 500kV sheet applies the same cost-per-kW logic at the level of the entire high-voltage “backbone”: the portfolio of 500kV projects divided by the regionwide load growth those projects enable. The underlying principle (project cost divided by the additional load the project serves) is identical in both. In the 2025 workbook, the final addition of the two pieces happens right on the “500kV Marginal Cost Adder” tab (the “Total Marginal Cost” line) rather than on a separate Summary tab.

In Summary
Every year the same idea is at work: (1) find where the system runs out of room; (2) price the fix; (3) see how much additional load that fix serves; and (4) divide one by the other to get a cost per kilowatt. Afterwards, remove statistical outliers and average across all locations, adjusting for inflation. That average is the AIC value. Beginning in 2025 a 500kV “backbone” adder, the total 500kV investment divided by the regionwide load growth it enables, is added on top to give the total Marginal Cost of Transmission.

===== DKT 56765 STF-JKA-10-11&12 PD/STF-JKA-10-11 PUBLIC DISCLOSURE.docx =====
STF-JKA-10-11

Question: 

Refer to STF-JKA-8-5.

a. Please explain how the Company’s 2023, 2024, and 2025 reliability price ($/kW-yr) was derived. Provide all supporting workpapers, memos, calculations, deriving the values provided in cell E3 of each tab.
b. Provide the load forecast for each year 2023-2025 used to set the values in cells D1 and E4. Please explain how the determination of the threshold capacity scalar was set to achieve approximately 50 hours per year.
c. Please explain the sum response capacity value amount in cell E5. How is this value determined?
d. Based on the actual RTP prices derived in 2023, please confirm that the input value of $xxxxx/kW-yr summed up over all the realized reliability components results in an annual price of approximately $ xxxxx /kW-yr for an RTP-DA customer that uses the same amount of energy in every assessed reliability hour of the year.

Response:

Please see STF-JKA-10-11 Attachments A - G.

Please see STF-JKA-10-11 Attachment H. The Reliability Threshold is set by ranking all 8,760/8,784 hourly loads for the forecast year from highest to lowest and selecting the 50th highest value as the threshold. Any hour with a load above this value will incur a Reliability Cost, while hours at or below this value will not. This approach directly ensures that approximately 50 hours per year will trigger Reliability pricing on a weather normal basis. 

The Reliability Sum Response is calculated by adding up, for each hour that exceeds the threshold, the amount by which that hour's load (as a percentage of peak) surpasses the threshold percentage. This sum serves as a scaling factor that distributes the $/kW-year reliability cost across qualifying hours in proportion to how far each hour exceeded the threshold, not just whether it exceeded.

The Reliability Price of $xxxxx/kW-yr is designed to recover the value of capacity based on forecasted, weather normal hourly loads. The $ xxxxx/kW-yr represents the amount recovered based on actual hourly loads and actual weather for 2023.

===== DKT 56765 STF-JKA-10-11&12 PD/STF-JKA-10-12.docx =====
STF-JKA-10-12

Question: 

Refer to STF-JKA-8-5.

a.Please provide the same workpaper derivations for the transmission component of the DA and HA RTP rates. Specifically provide the workpaper(s) that assigns a transmission cost and the scalars required to estimate the load threshold to target the highest 300 load hours of the year.
b.Please explain the source of any transmission costs used in the derivation. Provide all workpapers, memos, calculations deriving the values.
c.Please provide the load forecast used to the set the threshold capacity scalar to achieve approximately 300 hours per year.
d.Please explain the derivation of response capacity value, if applicable, used in the derivation.

Response:

Please see STF-JKA-10-12 Attachment A.

Please see STF-JKA-10-12 Attachments B - G.

Please see STF-JKA-10-11 Attachment H in the Company’s response to STF-JKA-10-11.  

The Transmission Sum Response is calculated by adding up, for each hour that exceeds the threshold, the amount by which that hour’s load (as a percentage of peak) surpasses the threshold percentage. Also, hours that exceed the threshold are weighted by a temperature factor to reflect the load carrying capability of the transmission system. The resulting sum serves as a scaling factor that distributes the $/kW-year transmission cost across qualifying hours in proportion to how far each hour exceeded the threshold, not just whether it exceeded.
